items.title: James Moody — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Eddie Jefferson came with me... he traveled with me... I made him the manager... I had Eddie Jefferson and me.

ctx.x: And how long did that group stay together?

Oh, a pretty good while. I'm bad at dates, but then after that I got a phone -- what I did was I did standards. 'Cause Eddie Jefferson came with me, you know. Babs [phonetic sp.] was with me singing, and then Babs got funny. "I wanna," you know, "I'm singing this song," said, "And I want more money." You know. And, see, when you talk like that, that's not the way to talk to people. Say, well, "Oh, no! I want my money and if I don't get it, I'm quitting!" That's what was said. And my response was, "Good bye."

items.title: James Moody interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998
items.q: His 1949 recording of “Moody’s Mood for Love” became a classic and he was covered by vocalists Eddie Jefferson and King Pleasure.

ctx.x: James Moody’s musical skills and engaging personality have made him one of the great stars of the jazz world. He was born in Savannah, Georgia on May 26, 1925, and was raised in Newark, New Jersey and Reading, Pennsylvania. He took up the saxophone at age 16 and gained valuable playing experience in the Air Force, where he met and played with Dizzy Gillespie. James became a member of Dizzy’s Be Bop Orchestra and he enjoyed a long relationship with the trumpet master. His 1949 recording of “Moody’s Mood for Love”…

James is one of the premier jazz flautists and most of his solo albums include a song featuring his unique vocal style. He has been honored by the Newark, NJ, Jamaica and the International Jazz Hall of Fame organizations. James lives in San Diego with his wife and manager Linda Moody.
